_about: Plain-language pass (2026-11-25): simpler explanations, feedback, learning objectives, long answer choices, question wording and activity instructions. Applied by Tools/apply_plain_language.ps1 to Assets/Editor/CurriculumQuestions.json, Docs/Curriculum_Question_Bank.md and Tools/activity_content.py so a regeneration keeps the same text. Correct answers, choice order, IDs and curriculum links are unchanged.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality means keeping information private. A stranger can now read Ana's grades and messages, so her privacy is broken. Integrity would mean her data was changed. Availability would mean she was locked out.
questions.feedback: Confidentiality! Ana's info wasn't changed or locked. It was seen by someone who shouldn't see it.
questions.objective: Name the security goal that a scam breaks.

questions.explanation: You didn't order anything, so there is no package. The text comes from a random mobile number, rushes you with a 12-hour deadline, and links to a site that isn't the courier's. The small fee is bait to get your card or e-wallet details.
questions.feedback: Scam! No order + a small fee + a rush deadline = a fake delivery text. Don't tap the link.
questions.objective: Spot a fake delivery text: unexpected, rushed, a small fee and a strange link.

questions.explanation: Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into giving away your password. This one copies the school (uphs1 uses the number 1, not the letter l), scares you with a deadline and asks you to sign in. Real storage warnings never ask for your password.
questions.feedback: Phishing! Look closely: uphs1, not uphsl. Fake sender + scary deadline + "sign in here" = phishing.
questions.objective: Name phishing and spot a fake look-alike address.

questions.explanation: A one-time code (OTP) is like a key: whoever has it can approve payments as you. A real bank never asks you to read it out. Hang up and call the number on your card, a number you already trust.
questions.feedback: Hang up! No real bank asks for your OTP. Call back on the number on your card.
questions.objective: Never share an OTP, and call back on a number you trust.

questions.explanation: A safe program never needs your antivirus turned off. Fake "free skins" tools often hide malware that steals your saved passwords. Scanning afterwards is too late, and sending it to a friend puts them at risk.
questions.feedback: Don't run it! When someone asks you to turn off your antivirus, they want to get past it.
questions.objective: Treat any request to turn off security tools as a warning sign.

questions.explanation: Pet names, old streets and birth months are common answers to password-reset questions. Posting them gives scammers what they need to get into your accounts. The "fun game" is how they collect them.
questions.feedback: Scam! Those are common security-question answers. Keep them off public posts.
questions.objective: Know that fun-looking posts can collect your personal info.

questions.explanation: A raffle only needs a way to contact you, not your ID and birthdate. Together, those can be used to pretend to be you. The Data Privacy Act says they must explain why they collect data and take only what they need.
questions.feedback: Too much! An ID photo for a raffle? Ask why they need it and look for a privacy notice.
questions.objective: Share personal data only when it's really needed and the reason is explained.

questions.explanation: "Forgot password" links go to your email. Whoever controls your email can reset your other accounts: social media, e-wallets and school. Protect it first with a unique password and MFA (a second check, like a code).
questions.feedback: Your email is the master key. Every "Forgot password" link goes there.
questions.objective: Protect first the account that unlocks all the others.

questions.explanation: This is a tech-support scam. Real warnings come from your computer's own security app, not from a web page with a phone number. The "support" person will ask for money or control of your PC. Close the tab. If it's stuck, close the browser with Task Manager.
questions.feedback: Scam! Real alerts come from your computer's settings, never from a web page that tells you to call.
questions.objective: Know where real security alerts come from.

questions.explanation: Proof is what lets PayLite and the police help you, and the reference number can help trace the money. Deleting the chat destroys proof. Public threats can get you in trouble. "Pay more to get a refund" is a second scam.
questions.feedback: Save the proof first: chat, profile and reference number. Then report it.
questions.objective: Save proof before doing anything else.

questions.explanation: You asked for this reset yourself a minute ago. The address matches the trusted one exactly, and it doesn't ask for your password. It even says you can ignore it if you didn't ask. Not every message is a scam!
questions.feedback: Legitimate! You asked for it, the address matches, and it doesn't ask for your password.
questions.objective: Real messages exist too: check the facts before calling something a scam.

questions.explanation: To find the real website, read the address from right to left, up to the first single "/". Here it is account-verify.example. The "examplebank" in front is a decoy the scammer added. Nothing is misspelled, and HTTPS doesn't make it safe.
questions.feedback: Read right to left: the real site is account-verify.example. The bank's name is just a decoy.
questions.objective: Find the real website in a link by reading right to left.

questions.explanation: The padlock (HTTPS) means your connection is private, so others can't read what you send. It doesn't say who owns the site. Anyone can get a padlock, scam sites too, so you still need to check the address.
questions.feedback: Padlock = private connection, not safe site. Fake sites have padlocks too.
questions.objective: Know that a padlock doesn't mean a site is real.

questions.explanation: A "family member" with a new number, a sudden emergency, a money request and "don't call me" are classic signs. This trick is called social engineering: it uses your feelings, not hacking. Call Migs's old number, or ask something only he would know.
questions.feedback: Impersonation! New number + emergency + "don't call" = call the old number first.
questions.objective: Spot scams that use feelings and rush you, and check through a number you know.

questions.explanation: Act fast. Changing your password makes the stolen one useless, and IT can block the fake site and warn others. Hiding it gives the attacker time. Forwarding spreads the bad link, and deleting removes the proof IT needs.
questions.feedback: Report it! Mistakes happen. Hiding them is what makes them worse.
questions.objective: Report a security mistake quickly and honestly.

questions.explanation: MFA (multi-factor authentication) asks for a second check, like a code or an app prompt, as well as the password. So a stolen password alone isn't enough. The other choices don't stop someone logging in from far away. Only approve prompts you started yourself.
questions.feedback: MFA! A stolen password alone isn't enough, as long as you never approve a prompt you didn't start.
questions.objective: Pick the protection that fits the problem.

questions.explanation: Two networks with almost the same name can mean one is a fake hotspot (an "evil twin"). No Wi-Fi needs your social media password: that page is stealing it. A VPN wouldn't help, because you'd still be typing your password into a fake page.
questions.feedback: Fake hotspot! No Wi-Fi needs your social media password. Ask staff, or use mobile data.
questions.objective: Spot fake Wi-Fi hotspots, and know what a VPN can't do.

questions.explanation: Scammers can fake the sender name on a text, so it can land in your real bank's chat. Look at the link instead: examplebank-ph.example isn't the bank's real site, and "suspended TODAY" is pressure. Many banks don't send links by text at all.
questions.feedback: Scam! Sender names can be faked. Check the link: it's not examplebank.example.
questions.objective: Know that the name on your phone doesn't prove who sent a text.

questions.explanation: This is pretexting: a made-up story that uses an important name and a rush to make you skip the rules. Sending a reset to a personal email could hand the account to a scammer. Always check first. A real dean will understand.
questions.feedback: Check first! Important person + rush is an old trick. Call back on the official number.
questions.objective: Follow the checking steps, even when someone important is rushing you.

questions.explanation: A .docm file can hold macros, which are small hidden programs. Office turns them off to keep you safe. Clicking "Enable Content" runs the scammer's program. A grades file doesn't need macros to show grades.
questions.feedback: Macro trap! Enable Content = run their program. Grades don't need macros.
questions.objective: Don't click "Enable Content" on unexpected attachments.

questions.explanation: The scammer studied your org's public page first, then wrote an email just for you. That is spear phishing: a fake message aimed at one person. Real details don't prove a real sender. The giveaways: a free-mail address, a "new account" and a same-day deadline.
questions.feedback: Spear phishing! They read your public page first. Real details don't mean a real sender.
questions.objective: Know that personal details can come from public pages and don't prove who sent a message.

questions.explanation: This trick doesn't steal your password. It gets you to give a fake app full access to your mail. A document viewer has no reason to send or delete emails. Changing your password later won't remove the app: you have to remove it from your account.
questions.feedback: Cancel! The sign-in was real, but the permissions were the trap. A viewer doesn't need to send your mail.
questions.objective: Read what an app asks for before you click Allow.

questions.explanation: The director's account may be controlled by a scammer, so the email passes every check. Replying just reaches the scammer. Zero trust means "never trust, always check", especially when bank details change. "Don't call" is a warning sign.
questions.feedback: Check by phone, on a number you already have. A real account can still be used by a scammer.
questions.objective: Double-check risky requests another way, even from trusted accounts.

questions.explanation: Fix first the problem that is most likely to happen and would do the most damage. The admin password is already public and has no MFA, so breaking in is easy, and that account controls everyone's email. The others matter, but they are less urgent.
questions.feedback: Admin account first: public password + no MFA + full control = most likely and most harmful.
questions.objective: Fix risks by how likely and how harmful they are.

questions.explanation: Investigators can only trust evidence that is complete and unchanged. Cropping hides context, and blurring hides the scammer's name they need. Keeping the original and noting when you saved each item is called the chain of custody. Uninstalling may delete the chat.
questions.feedback: Keep the originals untouched, share copies, and note when you saved each one.
questions.objective: Keep evidence complete, unchanged and recorded.

questions.explanation: The "From" name can say anything. SPF and DMARC are checks that ask: did the school's own mail system really send this? Both failed. Reply-To also sends your answer to the scammer. The subject and the time are only weak clues.
questions.feedback: SPF and DMARC failed, and replies go to free-mail. The "From" name is just text anyone can type.
questions.objective: Trust an email's hidden checks, not just what it shows.

questions.explanation: Real scholarships may ask for an ID, which makes this tricky. But no one needs your MPIN to send you money, and an ID plus a selfie holding it is all a scammer needs to open accounts as you. There is no privacy notice and only a mobile number, so check with the scholarship office directly.
questions.feedback: Scam! No one needs your MPIN to pay you. With your ID, selfie and MPIN, they can become you.
questions.objective: Tell a normal data request from identity theft.

questions.explanation: First, stop it spreading: cut the network so it can't reach other PCs. Leave the PC on so investigators keep the evidence. Paying doesn't promise your files back, restarting can erase evidence, and a USB can carry the infection.
questions.feedback: Disconnect, keep it on, report. Stop the spread first. Investigators need the evidence.
questions.objective: Know the first steps: stop the spread, keep the evidence, report.

questions.explanation: This is QR code phishing. The sticker over the real code is the clue you can see. A real payment QR opens inside your e-wallet app and shows the shop's name. It never asks for your MPIN on a web page. Tell the canteen staff too.
questions.feedback: Scam! A sticker, a web page and an MPIN request. Real payments happen inside the app.
questions.objective: Treat QR codes like links, and look for stickers placed on top.

questions.explanation: Using stolen passwords, even to help, is not allowed and can hurt the victims more. Posting the link sends more people to the fake page, and testing it gives away your own password. Report it: IT has the right to act. (ACM Code of Ethics: avoid harm, respect privacy, use only what you're allowed to.)
questions.feedback: Report it, don't touch it. Good intentions don't make using stolen data okay.
questions.objective: Report wrongdoing without causing more harm.
